 The Alligator’s governor voter guide
 Byron Donalds and David Jolly in close fight to be Florida’s leader
 By Alexa Ryan 
 October 30, 2026 | 11:59am EDT 
 Byron Donalds and David Jolly are the two candidates on the ballot for Florida Governor this year.
 Photo by Bayden Armstrong |
 and Noah Lantor 
 The Independent Florida Alligator
 For the first time in eight years, Gov. Ron DeSantis is not on the ballot for governor. Now, the big question is who will replace him, with a tight race less than a week before election day. 
 David Jolly , the Democratic candidate, and Byron Donalds , the Republican candidate, are within four percentage points of each other, according to a recent poll conducted by The New York Times and Siena Research Institute between Oct. 19 and Oct. 25.
 The poll shows Jolly with 44% of the vote compared to Donalds’ 48%.
 Early voting in Alachua County ended Nov. 1, and the polls will be open from 7 a.m. to 7 p.m. on Election Day.
 Jolly previously served in the U.S. House of Representatives from 2014 to 2017 as a Republican before switching to an independent in 2018. He frequently criticized President Donald Trump while serving as a political analyst for NBC and MSNBC, now MS NOW.
 He registered as a Democrat in April 2025. If elected, Jolly would be the first Democratic governor in Florida since 1999. His running mate, Gwen Graham, served in the U.S. House from 2015 to 2017. Graham is the daughter of former Florida governor Bob Graham.
 Donalds is currently serving in the U.S. House, representing Florida’s 19th Congressional district. He previously served in the Florida House from 2016 to 2020. If elected, Donalds would be the first Black governor in Florida history. His running mate, Bryan Ávila, left his post as a Florida state senator to join Donalds’ campaign.
 Donalds beat out Jay Collins, the current Florida lieutenant governor, for the Republican nomination during the Aug. 18 primary election. 
 Both candidates have notable endorsements. Former President Barack Obama endorsed Jolly, and Trump endorsed Donalds.
 Neither candidate responded to The Alligator’s questionnaire, but they have both publicly shared their views on Florida’s top issues.
 Here is where each candidate stands based on their campaign websites, past legislative work and public statements.
 Q. Affordability is consistently rated as a top concern among Florida voters. What specific policies do you plan to enact if you are elected to address this issue?

 Subscribe Now 
 David Jolly: Jolly’s plan to reduce insurance costs for Florida homeowners has been one of his most hotly debated campaign promises. He proposed removing wind risk from the private insurance market by creating a state catastrophe fund to bear it so insurance companies don’t factor it into premium costs. He’s claimed it would save homeowners 60% to 70% when paying insurance premiums. 
 However, a PolitiFact investigation published insurance experts’ claims that it’s unlikely it will save homeowners in the long run as the fund is depleted.
 Jolly also plans to expand Medicaid to help Floridians save on healthcare.
 Byron Donalds: Donalds plans to reduce insurance costs by cracking down on lawsuit abuse and protecting reforms that prevent false claims, which he says increase premiums for everyone. He also suggests cutting the red tape that slows rebuilding after a storm. 
 Donalds supports Amendment 3, which would increase the homestead property tax exemption for homeowners, as part of his affordability agenda. However, the municipalities that rely on those property taxes for services like libraries, fire services and natural disaster relief argue it would be detrimental to local communities. 
 Q. How would you describe yourself as a political candidate?
 David Jolly: Jolly is a moderate Democrat who often identifies as a centrist. 
 Byron Donalds: Donalds advertises himself as a “Conservative Warrior” and Trump-endorsed candidate on his campaign website. However, his support for Trump stirred doubt in September when he removed “Enact the Trump agenda” from his top priorities list on his campaign website. In an X post , he said the move reflected his shift toward focusing on his own agenda rather than a sign he was abandoning the Trump agenda.
 Q. What are your top three policy ideas?
 David Jolly: Jolly lists affordability, education and a pause on data center development as his top priorities. He plans to address affordability through an expansion of Medicaid and his hurricane insurance proposal.
 Within education, he wants to increase investment in public schools and create stricter requirements for private school vouchers.
 He has also taken a strong stance against data center development, promising an immediate one-year pause on data centers if elected.
 Byron Donalds: Donalds lists affordability, education and law and order as his top three priorities.
 On affordability, Donalds has advocated for Amendment 3 to lower property taxes, more checks on insurance companies to lower premiums and cutting red tape to make development cheaper and faster.
 On education, Donalds advocated for school choice, an expansion of the private school voucher program and greater parental supervision over learning materials. He also proposed early literacy programs to improve reading skills, connecting students with apprenticeships in trades so they can find employment straight out of high school and personalized success plans for every student starting in sixth grade.
 As part of his law and order agenda, Donalds said he supports a crackdown on illegal immigration.
 “Cut off state funds, subsidies, and free perks that encourage illegal immigration into Florida,” his campaign website said.
 He added that businesses should be required to use an E-Verify system to ensure that legal immigrants can keep their jobs and get paid. Additionally, Donalds said he wanted to target fentanyl by creating harsher punishments for the drug cartels that bring it into Florida.
 Q. What experience do you have that makes you the most qualified for the job?
 David Jolly: Jolly served in the U.S. House from 2014 to 2017 as a Republican, after working as a lobbyist.
 Byron Donalds: Donalds currently serves in the U.S. House representing part of Southwest Florida in the state’s 19th congressional district. He served in the Florida House from 2016 to 2020.
 Q. How will you balance economic growth and fiscal responsibility? And, what specific investments do you plan to make in Florida?
 David Jolly: Jolly’s campaign website focuses on four pillars to improve Florida’s economy: 
 Investing in infrastructure that attracts people who can make the state a leading technology hub.
 Strengthening the agriculture industry by using sustainable practices and supporting farms.
 Investing in tourism by maintaining the state’s workforce, infrastructure and environment.
 Balancing opportunity with innovation by attracting people to Florida while also keeping the state’s top talent.
 Byron Donalds: Donalds advocates for less regulation and more development by cutting bureaucratic regulations that slow economic and infrastructure growth. He specifically proposed a public shot clock for building permits to force public officials to more quickly approve applications. He also advocates for cutting taxes at every opportunity and adding technology-driven systems to weed out fraud and waste in the government’s spending.
 Donalds wants to make Florida a major technology and financial hub by investing in and supporting commercial space growth and what he calls smart growth of artificial intelligence infrastructure. Donalds has said he supports making data centers pay their own way by preventing them from passing their water and electricity costs onto residents.
 Q. What are your thoughts on the Safeguard American Voter Eligibility (SAVE) Act?
 David Jolly: Jolly’s stance on the SAVE Act is unclear. 
 However, the Democratic Party of Florida, of which he is a member, took a strong stance against it.
 Byron Donalds: Donalds supports the SAVE Act.
 “Well, the SAVE Act is very simple. It requires that for federal elections, in order to register to vote, to be eligible, you have to demonstrate that you are an American citizen. Very simple,” he said in 2025 when it was being discussed in Congress. “Protect the franchise of voting for Americans in our country.”
